canonical_topic: Round-trip efficiency and storage breakeven economics
definition: Storage facilities lose energy converting electricity into another form and back; the resulting round-trip efficiency sets the minimum peak/off-peak price spread needed just to break even on gross profit, before any capital or maintenance costs.
core_idea: With a 25% round-trip efficiency, only one unit of electricity is recovered for every four units put in, so peak prices would need to be at least four times off-peak prices just to break even on gross margin — and that still ignores installation and ongoing maintenance costs.
key_points: Author's example: a storage facility with 25% efficiency returns only 25% of the electricity put into it.
At 25% efficiency, peak prices consistently four times off-peak prices would let the system break even on gross profit only.
Breaking even on gross profit does not cover installation and ongoing maintenance costs, so real-world viability requires an even wider spread.
relationships: Electricity storage as a price-arbitrage opportunity
trading_implications: When valuing a storage asset, compare the observed peak/off-peak spread to 1/efficiency to see if there is room for gross profit before fixed costs.
Low round-trip-efficiency technologies need very wide, reliable price spreads to be economic at all.
caveats: Breaking even on gross profit is not the same as a profitable investment — capital and maintenance costs still have to be covered on top.

formulas.name: Storage breakeven price ratio
formulas.formula: Breakeven Peak/Off-Peak Price Ratio = 1 / Round-Trip Efficiency

variables.Round-Trip Efficiency: fraction of stored electricity recovered after storage losses (e.g., 0.25 = 25%)
